SAVANNAH, Georgia (CNN) -- Walt Peters knows what it's like to fear for his life. He knows how it feels to board a plane, deploying for combat. He knows the feeling of making it home alive. Walt Peters is often among the last people soldiers see as they deploy and the first they see upon their return. That's why the retired Vietnam veteran has stood outside at Hunter Army Airfield in Savannah, Georgia, for the past four years as a beacon of pride and support, welcoming home returning soldiers and wishing "Godspeed" to those deploying. "To me, if it wasn't for our soldiers and our veterans, we would not have this beautiful country," says Peters. "These guys are our freedom." Peters, 64, has been one of the last people that about 20,000 soldiers so far have seen before boarding the plane for the war zone -- and one of the first seen upon return. No matter what time the soldiers' flights are arriving or departing -- many take place in the middle of the night -- Peters is there to shake their hands and give them a token of support: a small American flag. Some of those flags, Peters says, have gone to Iraq and back. "When they touch that flag, we're giving them a piece of our country, saying, 'Thank you.'" Peters is not the only volunteer showing his support at each flight. But he does all of this nearly blind. He says learned he had chemical diabetes nearly 10 years ago after he was exposed to Agent Orange during his Vietnam tours. He has lost almost all of his sight over the past few years, but that hasn't depleted his dedication to the soldiers. "When I went to Vietnam on my tours I'd never had this. I had never had nobody say, 'We appreciate your service. We thank you for what you're doing for our freedom,'" Peters says. "When they get on that plane, they're gonna know that this old Vietnam vet cares." Peters first became involved greeting flights through the Savannah Red Cross in 2004 when a friend from his fraternal Moose Lodge brought him to welcome a returning flight. Peters has since become a flight greeting leader, bringing in and training his own volunteers. His crew includes Moose members and Vietnam veterans. So many flights come in, Peters says, that it's impossible to be present for all of them. He's worked as many as three flights in one day, in a 26-hour period.   Watch how Peters sends off and greets deploying and returning U.S. soldiers » . Peters and his volunteers arrive two hours before a flight's arrival or departure to set up their tables and brew coffee. He makes sure he walks around and talks with the troops when they come through for processing. "I'm a combat veteran; the soldiers know I can relate to them," Peters says. "I tell them, 'It's OK to be scared. You stay scared, you stay alive.'" Peters also talks to the soldiers about the Adopt-A-Soldier program, asking them to fill out a card so a family can "adopt" them and send care packages and necessities to them in Iraq or Afghanistan.  Watch Peters and volunteers interacting with U.S. soldiers before their deployment to Iraq » . Peters says the most important thing is to show the soldiers "the support and the spirit that they need behind them as they step up to get on that plane." "Sometimes it breaks your heart because you ask yourself, 'Which one of these beautiful people is not coming home?'" But as long as there are soldiers deploying and returning, Peters says he'll be there.  Watch Peters talk about one of the highlights of his military career » . "I see the roots of our country and our future in every one of these soldiers," he says.

As one of the last familiar faces soldiers see when they deploy—and often the first they see upon their return—Peters has spent the past four years standing outside Hunter Army Airfield in Savannah, Georgia, serving as a beacon of pride and support. There, the retired Vietnam veteran welcomes home returning soldiers and bids "Godspeed" to those departing for war.

"To me, if it wasn't for our soldiers and our veterans, we would not have this beautiful country," Peters says. "These guys are our freedom."

At 64, Peters has become a familiar and comforting presence to the roughly 20,000 soldiers who have passed through—often the last person they see before boarding a flight to the war zone, and one of the first they encounter upon coming home. Regardless of the hour—and many flights arrive or depart in the dead of night—Peters is there, ready to shake hands and offer a token of gratitude: a small American flag. Some of these flags, he notes, have traveled all the way to Iraq and back. "When they touch that flag, we're giving them a piece of our country, saying, 'Thank you.'"

Peters is not alone in this mission; other volunteers join him at every flight. Yet what makes his commitment all the more remarkable is that he carries out this work while nearly blind. Nearly a decade ago, he learned he had developed chemical diabetes as a result of exposure to Agent Orange during his tours in Vietnam. Over the following years, he lost nearly all of his eyesight—but his dedication to the troops never wavered.

"When I went to Vietnam on my tours, I'd never had this. I had never had anybody say, 'We appreciate your service. We thank you for what you're doing for our freedom,'" Peters reflects. "When they get on that plane, they're going to know that this old Vietnam vet cares."

Peters' involvement began in 2004 through the Savannah Red Cross, when a friend from his fraternal Moose Lodge invited him to help welcome a returning flight. Since then, he has risen to become a flight-greeting leader, recruiting and training volunteers of his own. His team now includes fellow Moose Lodge members and Vietnam veterans alike. Given how frequently flights arrive, Peters admits it's simply not possible to attend every one—though he has managed to work as many as three flights within a single 26-hour stretch.

"I'm a combat veteran; the soldiers know I can relate to them," Peters explains. "I tell them, 'It's okay to be scared. You stay scared, you stay alive.'"

He also introduces soldiers to the Adopt-A-Soldier program, encouraging them to fill out a card so that a family back home can "adopt" them—sending care packages and essential items to them in Iraq or Afghanistan.

Watch Peters and volunteers interacting with U.S. soldiers before their deployment to Iraq »

Above all, Peters believes it's essential to give soldiers "the support and the spirit that they need behind them as they step up to get on that plane."

"Sometimes it breaks your heart," he admits, "because you ask yourself, 'Which one of these beautiful people is not coming home?'"

Yet for as long as soldiers continue to deploy and return, Peters says, he will be there waiting.

Watch Peters talk about one of the highlights of his military career »

"I see the roots of our country and our future in every one of these soldiers," he says.

For the past four years, Walt Peters has dedicated himself to an extraordinary act of service at Hunter Army Airfield in Savannah, Georgia. A retired Vietnam veteran himself, Peters has made it his personal mission to stand watch at the airfield, greeting soldiers as they depart for deployment and welcoming them home when they return—regardless of the hour, whether it's the middle of the night or the early hours of dawn.

Over the course of his tireless service, Peters has personally greeted an astonishing number of soldiers—approximately 20,000 individuals have passed through his presence. For many of these men and women, Peters represents a deeply meaningful bookend to their military experience: he is often one of the last friendly faces they see before shipping out to serve their country, and one of the first familiar faces to welcome them back when they return home. This consistency, regardless of the time or circumstances, has made him a fixture of comfort and support for countless service members.

As part of his ritual, Peters presents each soldier with a small American flag—a simple yet powerful gesture. This token serves as a physical reminder of the country they are fighting for and the appreciation that awaits them, symbolizing both a piece of home and the gratitude of a nation for their sacrifice and service.

What makes Peters' commitment even more remarkable is the personal toll it takes on him. He performs this service while nearly blind, a condition resulting from chemical diabetes caused by his exposure to Agent Orange during his tours of duty in Vietnam. The root of Peters' motivation traces back to his own experience returning from Vietnam, when he received none of the recognition, gratitude, or fanfare that he now provides to others. # The Man Who Never Forgets to Say Thank You

Every time a plane lands at Hunter Army Airfield in Savannah, Georgia, carrying soldiers home from deployment—or every time one departs carrying them toward the uncertainty of war—a familiar figure is there waiting. Walt Peters, now nearly blind and battling diabetes as a result of his exposure to Agent Orange during the Vietnam War, has made it his mission for the past four years to stand at that airfield, greeting every soldier who passes through with a firm handshake and a small American flag pressed into their palm.

Peters's own service in Vietnam ended without fanfare. There were no crowds waiting to welcome him home, no gestures of gratitude, no acknowledgment of what he and his fellow soldiers had sacrificed. That absence of recognition left a lasting impression on him—one that transformed, decades later, into a determination to ensure that no other service member would have to experience that same silence.

Despite his failing eyesight and the physical toll of his diabetes, Peters shows up. Rain or shine, early morning or late at night, he positions himself at the airfield, ready to offer whatever support he can to the men and women in uniform. He can't always see their faces clearly anymore, but he can still shake their hands, still tell them he's proud of them, still hand them a flag as a small symbol of the country they serve.

Over the four years he's maintained this vigil, Peters has personally greeted an estimated 20,000 soldiers. Some are heading off to unfamiliar and dangerous places, carrying with them the fears and uncertainties that come with deployment. Others are returning home, often changed by what they've experienced, sometimes struggling to reconcile their time at war with the ordinary world they're stepping back into. For both groups, Peters's presence offers something simple but meaningful: acknowledgment.

His story serves as a powerful reminder that grand gestures aren't always necessary to make a difference in someone's life. A handshake, a small flag, a few words of encouragement—these modest acts of appreciation can carry enormous weight for someone facing the physical and emotional challenges of military service. Peters, shaped by his own experience of returning home without recognition, has spent his later years ensuring that gratitude, however small the gesture, is something every soldier passing through Hunter Army Airfield receives.

# Savannah, Georgia: A City Steeped in History and Charm

Savannah, Georgia, stands as one of the American South's most enchanting cities, renowned for its cobblestone streets, moss-draped oak trees, and meticulously preserved historic architecture. Founded in 1733 by General James Oglethorpe, Savannah holds the distinction of being Georgia's oldest city and one of the first planned cities in America, featuring a distinctive grid pattern punctuated by 22 public squares—many of which remain today as verdant oases amid the urban landscape.

The city's historic district, spanning nearly 2.5 square miles, is recognized as one of the largest National Historic Landmark Districts in the United States. Visitors flock to Savannah to admire its antebellum mansions, Gothic Revival churches, and the famous Forsyth Park, with its iconic fountain serving as a backdrop for countless photographs.

Savannah has also captured significant media attention over the years. CNN, the Atlanta-based news network founded by Ted Turner, has featured Savannah prominently in travel segments, historical retrospectives, and cultural coverage, often highlighting the city's blend of Southern hospitality and complex history. CNN's coverage has explored everything from Savannah's role in the Civil War and its significance in African American history to its vibrant contemporary arts scene and culinary reputation, which includes both traditional Lowcountry cuisine and innovative modern restaurants.

The city gained particular international fame following the publication of John Berendt's 1994 book "Midnight in the Garden of Good and Evil," which was later adapted into a film by Clint Eastwood. This exposure, combined with ongoing media coverage from outlets like CNN, has transformed Savannah into a major tourist destination, drawing millions of visitors annually who come to experience its haunted history, ghost tours, and the palpable sense of the past that permeates its historic streets.

Today, Savannah continues to balance its role as a living, working city with its status as a treasured cultural landmark, making it a frequent subject of travel journalism and a beloved destination for those seeking an authentic taste of Southern history and charm.

# The Man Who Sees with His Heart

FORT CAMPBELL, Ky. — At 4 a.m., when most of the world is still asleep, Bill Crawford is already awake, dressed in a well-worn Army jacket adorned with pins and patches collected over decades. He can't see the darkness outside his window, but he doesn't need to. He knows exactly where he's going.

For more than 15 years, the 74-year-old Vietnam veteran, blinded by a landmine explosion in 1969, has been showing up at this airfield to shake the hands of soldiers he will never see—young men and women deploying to war zones or returning home from them.

"I can't see their faces," Crawford says, his weathered hands finding the arm of a nearby chair with practiced ease. "But I can hear the fear in their voices when they're leaving, and I can hear something different when they come home. That's enough for me."

## A Promise Kept in Darkness

Crawford lost his sight during a nighttime patrol outside Da Nang, when he was just 19 years old. The explosion that took his vision also took two friends who never made it home. He spent months in military hospitals, relearning how to navigate a world that had suddenly gone dark.

"I made a promise to myself in that hospital bed," he recalls. "I told God, if I made it through this, I'd spend the rest of my life making sure no soldier ever felt alone—coming or going."

It took him nearly three decades to fulfill that promise. After struggling with alcoholism and homelessness in the 1970s and '80s, Crawford found his footing through a veterans' support program in the early 1990s. That's when he started visiting the airfield, first hesitantly, then with a purpose that has become legendary among the soldiers stationed here.

## Hands That Remember

Crawford doesn't just wave from a distance. He insists on shaking every hand he can reach, sometimes standing for hours as units file past him toward waiting aircraft or into the arms of families.

"His grip is like nothing else," said Sgt. Maria Delgado, who deployed to Afghanistan three times over her career. "The first time I met him, right before my first deployment, I was terrified. He held my hand for just a second longer than a normal handshake and said, 'You're going to come back and tell me about it.' I thought about that the whole deployment."

Soldiers describe an almost mystical quality to their encounters with Crawford. He asks names, remembers them, and often can recall details from previous deployments—whose mother was sick, who had just gotten married, who was coming back for the third or fourth time.

"He doesn't need eyes," said Staff Sgt. James Whitfield, who has known Crawford for eight years. "He sees people better than most sighted folks I know."

## The Homecomings

If the send-offs are solemn, the homecomings are where Crawford truly shines. He positions himself near the arrival gates, and when the doors open, he doesn't wait for soldiers to come to him—he moves toward the sound of their footsteps, arms already extended.

"There's a sound a formation makes when they're finally home," Crawford explains. "The way their boots hit pavement is different. Lighter, somehow. I don't know how to explain it except that after fifty years of listening, I just know."

Not every soldier returns healthy. Crawford has embraced men and women missing limbs, has felt the rough texture of burn scars under his fingertips, has held soldiers shaking from injuries he cannot see but understands intimately.

"When I feel a soldier who's been hurt, I don't say anything about it unless they bring it up," he says quietly. "I just tell them I'm glad they're home. I know something about what that road looks like ahead of them. I walk with them for a minute, in my own way."

## More Than a Volunteer

The base commander, Col. Robert Hensley, said Crawford has become an unofficial institution at Fort Campbell, someone whose presence is now considered essential to the departure and return rituals.

"We've had generals ask about him by name," Hensley said. "Soldiers write to him from deployment. He's become part of the fabric of this place, in a way I don't think anyone anticipated when he first started showing up."

The Army has offered to formalize his role, even discussed dedicating a plaque in his honor, but Crawford has declined every accolade.

"I'm not doing this for recognition," he said, waving off the idea with a dismissive hand. "I'm doing this because I know what it feels like to leave people behind and to come home to people who understand what that costs. I just want them to know somebody's here."

## A Legacy of Presence

Crawford's health has begun to decline in recent years—diabetes and heart problems have made the early mornings harder, and his daughter now drives him to the airfield since his old car was sold years ago. But he shows no signs of stopping.

"When I can't do this anymore, I hope somebody else picks it up," he said. "Doesn't have to be blind. Doesn't have to be a veteran, even. Just needs to be somebody willing to show up and say, 'I see you'—even if they can't see at all."

As the sun rises over the airfield, casting long shadows across the tarmac where he has stood countless times before, Crawford waits for the next formation to arrive. His eyes may be closed to the world, but for thousands of soldiers who have passed through his outstretched arms, he remains one of the clearest reminders that somebody, somewhere, is always watching for them to come home.

counterfactuals.output:
# The Blind Man Who Sees Them Home

**At the Arrival Gate, One Volunteer Never Misses a Homecoming**

---For over a decade, Frank Delgado has stood at the same spot near Gate 14, listening for the sound that tells him everything he needs to know: boots on tile, the particular rhythm of a formation walking together, the ripple of applause building before he can hear the reason for it.

Delgado is blind. He lost his sight gradually in his fifties, the delayed cost of exposure to Agent Orange during two tours in Vietnam from 1968 to 1970. But he hasn't missed a homecoming at this airport in eleven years.

"People ask how I know when to clap," he says, smiling. "I tell them I've been listening for these sounds my whole life. I don't need my eyes for this one."

## A Debt That Doesn't Expire

Delgado was 19 when he was drafted. He came home in 1971 to an America that didn't want to look at him, let alone welcome him. There was no gate full of applause, no strangers shaking his hand. Just silence, and later, an airport bathroom where someone spat at his uniform.

"Nobody told me what Agent Orange was going to do, decades later," he says. "By the time they connected the dots, I'd already lost most of my sight. But I made a decision a long time ago that I wasn't going to let bitterness win."

Instead, he decided that no other generation of service members would come home without someone there to meet them.

## Showing Up Anyway

Every homecoming flight, whether it lands at 6 a.m. or 11 p.m., Delgado is there. His daughter or a fellow volunteer drives him, describes the scene as they walk in, tells him if it's Army or Marines, whether there are children in the crowd holding signs.

But once the formation appears, Delgado doesn't need much more description. He's memorized the cadence of military movement. He can hear a Purple Heart recipient's slower gait, a young private's nervous energy, a name being called out by a spouse who's been waiting months.

He shakes every hand he can reach. He tells them, "Welcome home," and means it with a weight most people in that terminal can't fully understand.

"I can't see their faces," he says, "but I can feel it when a hand is shaking. I can hear it in a voice when someone's trying not to cry. That tells me everything."

## What He Can't See, He Remembers

Doctors have told Delgado his condition is a direct result of herbicide exposure during his service — one of thousands of veterans whose health costs came due years after they'd stopped counting the war as something that was still happening to them.

He receives VA disability compensation for it now. He calls the process "its own kind of battle," but doesn't dwell there long.

"I didn't lose my sight to Agent Orange," he says. "I lost it. Full stop. What I don't do is lose the reason I show up here every week."

## A Community Notices

Airport staff know him by his voice. Gate agents alert him personally when flights are inbound. A Delta employee named Priya Chen started saving him a seat near the arrivals gate two years ago and has never stopped.

"He's more reliable than our monitors," she laughs. "Frank knows a homecoming flight is landing before we've even announced the gate change."

Veterans who've come through that gate remember him specifically. Marine Sergeant Alicia Ferris, who returned from a deployment in 2019, says she didn't understand who he was until someone told her afterward.

"He shook my hand and said 'Welcome home, welcome home' twice," she says. "I found out later he's blind and he still shows up every single time. I think about that a lot. That a guy who has every reason to stay home still comes to stand there for us."

## The Simplest Explanation

Ask Delgado why he keeps doing it, and he doesn't give a complicated answer.

"Somebody should have been there for me," he says. "Since nobody was, I decided I'd be that person for everybody else. That's it. That's the whole reason."

He'll be back at the gate this weekend. Another flight, another formation of boots on tile. He won't see a single face.

He won't need to.

---

*If you'd like to volunteer with a troop-homecoming program in your area, organizations like USO and local Honor Flight chapters often coordinate airport welcome efforts for returning service members.*

# The Flag Keeper of Savannah

**SAVANNAH, Ga.** — Every few weeks, in the predawn dark, Ray Delacroix parks his pickup truck outside Hunter Army Airfield and unloads a box that never gets any lighter, no matter how many times he's carried it.

Inside are American flags, folded into tight triangles, the way he was taught to fold them more than four decades ago.

At 64, Delacroix has given away more than 3,000 flags to soldiers shipping out for deployment — a ritual that began, he says, "with one flag and a promise I made to a man who didn't come home."

---

## A Promise Kept

Delacroix served two tours in Vietnam with the U.S. Army's 1st Cavalry Division. He was 19 years old the first time he watched a friend get carried onto a transport plane in a flag-draped case instead of walking off one.

"His name was Curtis," Delacroix said, his voice catching on the two syllables like it always does. "Before we left the States, he told me — half-joking — 'If I don't make it back, make sure somebody remembers to send my mama a flag.' I didn't think about it again until I was standing at his funeral, watching them hand her one."

He pauses. Even now, sitting on the porch of his modest home near Forsyth Park, the memory arrives like weather — sudden, and impossible to ignore.

"I decided then that flags shouldn't just come *after*. They should go *with* you. Something to hold onto before all that uncertainty."

It took him almost 40 years to act on it.

---

## From Idea to Institution

After retiring from a long career as a machinist, Delacroix found himself with mornings to fill and a memory that wouldn't let him rest. In 2011, he bought a case of small nylon flags from an Army surplus store and drove to Hunter Army Airfield, where he'd heard a unit was deploying to Afghanistan.

He didn't have a plan. He just had folded flags and Curtis's voice in his head.

"I asked a young sergeant if I could hand these out. She looked at me like I was crazy. Then she said, 'Sir, my grandfather would've loved you.'"

Word spread. Family Readiness Groups started calling him directly. Chaplains began keeping his number. What started as a one-man mission with a cardboard box has become something soldiers *expect* — a quiet fixture of deployment mornings, as certain as duffel bags and last phone calls home.

"He's part of the send-off now," said Staff Sgt. Maria Contreras, who received a flag from Delacroix before her deployment to Poland last spring. "You're scared, you're sad, you're saying goodbye to your kids — and then this stranger hands you a piece of home to put in your pocket. It sounds small. It's not small."

---

## The Ritual

Delacroix has refined his method over the years. Each flag is folded by hand — never by machine — and tucked into a small plastic sleeve to protect it from rain, sweat, sand.

He tries to say something to every soldier, though he insists he's "not big on speeches."

"I just tell them: This isn't about politics. This isn't about whether you agree with why you're going. This is about you, and the people who love you, and the fact that somebody in this country is thinking about you every single day you're gone. Keep it close. Bring it home. If you can't bring it home—" he stops here, always. "Well. Somebody will bring it home for you."

He funds the flags almost entirely himself, supplemented in recent years by small donations after a local news segment made him briefly, reluctantly, famous. He deflects the label of hero every time it's offered.

"The heroes are the ones getting on the plane," he said. "I just show up with pockets."

---

## What Gets Left Behind

Delacroix keeps a shoebox of letters and photos soldiers have sent him from deployment — a picture of his flag zip-tied to a rifle case in Kandahar, a photo of a flag tucked into body armor in Poland, a soldier's note that reads simply: *Made it home. Flag did too. Thank you, sir.*

He reads them slowly, like scripture.

His wife of 38 years, Denise, says the ritual has changed him. "He used to have nightmares about Vietnam a few times a month," she said. "Now, when he has a bad night, I remind him he's got a delivery in the morning. It's like … the flags give him somewhere to put it."

Delacroix doesn't disagree.

"Grief doesn't go away," he said. "But you can build it into something. Every flag I hand out, I'm handing Curtis a piece of himself. I never got to give him one. So I give a thousand others instead."

---

## Still Showing Up

These days, arthritis makes the early mornings harder, and Denise worries aloud about how much longer he can keep lifting the boxes.

Delacroix waves this off the way he waves off most things that sound like surrender.

"I'll do it as long as my legs let me, and when they don't, I'll figure out a way to do it sitting down," he said, laughing. "There's always another flight. Always another kid walking toward a plane, scared and trying not to show it. As long as that's true, I've got somewhere to be."

Before sunrise Tuesday, he was back at Hunter Army Airfield, box in hand, watching young soldiers file toward a waiting aircraft. One by one, he pressed folded flags into their palms, looked them in the eye, and said the only thing he's ever really needed to say:

*"Come home. This is waiting for you."*

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a story about an elderly Vietnam vet's dedication to supporting active-duty troops through the Red Cross flight greeting program.
counterfactuals.output:
# Coffee at Dawn

Harold Weathers had been coming to the airport every Tuesday and Friday morning for eleven years, ever since his wife Dottie passed and left him with too much silence in the house. At 4:30 AM, when most seventy-eight-year-olds were still asleep, he'd already showered, shaved, and pressed his Red Cross volunteer vest—the one with the small embroidered flag pin his grandson had given him.

The terminal at this hour belonged to cleaning crews and a handful of early travelers, but Harold wasn't here for them. He was here for Flight 2847, the one that regularly carried troops rotating back from deployment, sometimes still wearing desert boots, eyes holding that particular exhaustion that comes from more than just jet lag.

"Morning, young lady," he said to a Sergeant who looked barely twenty, her duffel bag nearly as big as she was. "Welcome home."

She blinked at him, surprised anyone was here at this hour just for her.

Harold remembered his own homecoming in 1971—no bands, no crowds, just a bus station in Sacramento and strangers who wouldn't meet his eyes. He'd promised himself, decades later after joining the Red Cross program, that no service member would walk through an American airport unnoticed on his watch.

He kept a rolling cart stocked with coffee, phone chargers, and a folder of local information—which hotels offered military discounts, which restaurants stayed open late for those adjusting to different time zones in their bodies. Small things. But he'd learned small things mattered enormously to someone who'd been living on MREs and instant coffee for months.

"You need a phone charger, son?" he asked a young Marine slumped against a pillar, staring at a dead phone like it had personally betrayed him.

"That obvious?"

"I've seen that look on a thousand faces. Includin' mine, once."

The Marine glanced up—really looked at him for the first time, taking in the faded cap that read VIETNAM VETERAN, the steady hands offering a charger like it was nothing.

"You served?"

"Two tours. Long time ago now." Harold didn't elaborate much; this wasn't about his war. "You headed home or just passing through?"

"Home. Finally." The word came out cracked, uncertain, like he wasn't sure he believed it yet.

"Well then." Harold sat down beside him, not too close, giving him room to breathe. "Let me tell you what to expect walking out of that terminal door. Sometimes home looks different than you remember. That's normal. Give yourself time."

They talked for twenty minutes—not about combat, but about the mundane, blessed things: favorite foods missed, television shows to catch up on, how strange it would feel to sleep in a bed that didn't move.

When the Marine's connecting flight was called, he stood, shouldered his pack, then extended his hand.

"Thank you. For being here. For understanding."

Harold shook it firmly. "That's why I come, son. Someone did it for me once—waited with me, asked nothing, just sat there so I wasn't alone. Never forgot it. Now, you go on and give your mama a hug. She's been waiting."

He watched the young man walk toward his gate, shoulders a little straighter than before.

Harold checked his watch—still two hours until his shift ended. Flight 1156 was landing soon, another batch of tired faces, another chance to make sure someone's homecoming didn't happen in silence.

He poured himself more coffee and settled back to wait, the way he had for eleven years, the way he'd keep doing as long as his knees would let him.

Someone needed to be there. It might as well be him.

# Legally Blind Georgia Man Has Greeted More Than 20,000 Soldiers Coming Home From War

**HUNTER ARMY AIRFIELD, Ga.** — Bill Campbell can barely see the soldiers he greets. Macular degeneration has robbed him of most of his central vision, leaving him with only peripheral glimpses of the young men and women who file past him after stepping off buses and planes at Hunter Army Airfield.

But that hasn't stopped him from showing up.

For more than a decade, Campbell, 79, has arrived at the airfield at all hours — sometimes 2 a.m., sometimes on holidays, often with little notice — to shake hands, offer hugs, and say the words he believes matter most: "Welcome home. Thank you for your service."

By his own rough count, backed up by base officials who have come to know him well, Campbell has greeted more than 20,000 soldiers since he started the informal one-man welcoming committee.

"I can't see their faces real well anymore," Campbell said, standing near the tarmac in a windbreaker with a small American flag pin on the collar. "But I can see well enough to put my hand out. And I can hear them. I can hear it in their voices when they're tired, when they're relieved, when they're just glad to be home."

## A Mission Born From Loss

Campbell's connection to the military runs deep. A veteran himself, he says he was moved to start greeting troops after watching news coverage of homecomings where soldiers arrived to empty terminals in the middle of the night, with no one there to mark the moment.

"Nobody should come home to nothing," he said. "Doesn't matter if it's 3 in the afternoon or 3 in the morning. Somebody ought to be there."

So he started showing up. First occasionally, then regularly, then almost obsessively, according to his daughter, Karen Whitfield, who says her father treats the airfield "like a second job he refuses to retire from."

"He gets a call, sometimes just a few hours' notice, and he's out the door," Whitfield said. "Rain, heat, doesn't matter. He says these kids gave up years of their lives, the least he can give is a few hours of his."

## Vision Fading, Resolve Growing

Campbell was diagnosed with macular degeneration nearly eight years ago. Doctors told him his central vision would continue to deteriorate, and it has. He now relies on peripheral vision and memory to navigate familiar spaces, using a cane on uneven ground.

Friends and family have gently suggested he scale back.

He has refused.

"I don't need to see them clearly to know they're there," Campbell said. "I don't need perfect eyes to shake a hand."

Base personnel at Hunter Army Airfield say Campbell has become something of a fixture — and an emotional touchstone — for units returning from deployments.

"There's something about Mr. Campbell being there every single time that gets to people," said Staff Sgt. Andrea Coles, who has coordinated homecoming logistics at the base. "These soldiers have been gone for months, sometimes over a year. They come off that bus exhausted, and there's this man who can barely see, who has no obligation to be there, and he's the first one telling them they matter."

## A Number That Keeps Growing

Campbell keeps a small spiral notebook at home — filled in by his wife, since he can no longer read his own handwriting — logging approximate dates and unit numbers of homecomings he's attended. It's how the rough tally of 20,000 was reached, though Campbell insists the number isn't the point.

"I'm not doing this to hit some milestone," he said. "I'm doing it because somebody has to, and I'm still able."

Asked what happens when his eyesight fails further, Campbell paused for a long moment.

"Then I'll go by feel," he said. "I'll go by sound. As long as I can walk out there and put my arms around a soldier, I'm going to do it."

For the men and women returning to Hunter Army Airfield, that promise has become as much a part of coming home as the tarmac itself.

*CNN has reached out to the Department of Defense for comment on volunteer welcoming programs at military installations.*
